I had explored the idea of android app publishing earlier. However, I feel that the world of web-apps is also profitable, but I just need the right idea. I am a full-stack dev who knows everything on the stack right from bootstrap to jquery on the front-end and php/mysql to java on the backend.

But I am unable to find that yet unexplored area or niche that can pay well in the long term. I am not interested in anything BIG like a social media site, that's astronomical work for a solo dev. I want something on a micro scale for say small industries or startups. Here are a few ideas that already crossed my mind:

  1. Create a project workflow management app like Asana or Basecamp. I can use my creativity and build a workflow app, but is there even demand for it? There are already free tools like trello, then who will even use my app? How do I find pain points that users might be experiencing in these apps?

  2. Create an email distribution/marketing service. Again, mailchimp, aweber and many others have already saturated this field. I don't think there is even place for a new comer.

  3. Create an cloud-based accounting or ERP/CRM package like quickbooks. Though this market is saturated, I think there is scope for a new comer because accounting/ERP systems are a staple need and if I keep the price range low enough, I can get some users. But where I lack is that I just don't know how to approach these clients and do the marketing. There is also the question of identifying pain-points in existing products like quickbooks that I can fulfill (an obvious one is the price point).

Can someone give me more pointers abt this?
Which web-app idea(s) are relatively unexplored yet?

You said you're not after the next Big Idea. That's good. But in that case I would suggest looking towards existing business models. Find one that is profitable and go from there. Instead of searching for unexplored areas, embrace the explored. Let someone else do the grunt work. Stand on their shoulders.

Now I'm not advising stealing someone else's work. But if I were interested in creating an Android app--for example--I would find one that has a lot of paid downloads that I had the skill set and passion to improve upon. I would make needed changes and get in the game. You can do this with all kinds of ideas. Look at Zappos. It wasn't the first online shoe store. But that didn't stop Amazon from acquiring it and making its founders rich.

SaaS is good. Your cloud-based accounting idea is good. But something about it still sounds a little too broad. I don't know. I prefer to invest in businesses with a narrow scope and recurring revenue models. It can be such a headache to work on one big thing considering there are tons of little things available that require some initial upfront work but keep profits coming in. Android apps. YouTube videos. SaaS. Mailing lists. All good examples.

What I do know is that tech billionaire Chris Sacca said one of his most profitable ventures wasn't another Twitter or Uber-- it was a small hair salon that his wife encouraged him to invest in. So find something small and do it big. That's all I got.
